title: How to Teach Addition to Grade 1 (5 Strategies That Actually Work) + Free Quiz
meta_title: How to Teach Addition to Grade 1 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Five classroom-tested ways to teach Grade 1 addition, from counting-on to making ten, with a free 8-question online quiz and printable practice.
excerpt: Counting on fingers is where every six-year-old starts, but it is not where they should stay. Here are the five addition strategies I lean on with Grade 1, in the order that works, plus a quick quiz to test your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a class of six-year-olds to add 8 and 5 and you will see ten fingers go up, then a pause, then a lot of quiet counting. That is completely normal. The problem is that finger-counting stalls the moment the answer goes past ten, and by the second half of Grade 1 the sums do exactly that. So the real job in Grade 1 is not to make children add faster on their fingers — it is to move them, gently, off their fingers and onto strategies they can hold in their head.

Below are the five strategies I keep coming back to, roughly in the order a child should meet them. You do not need flashcards or an app. You need a handful of counters (buttons, beans, coins), ten minutes, and a bit of patience.

1. Counting on, not counting all

Most children start by counting all: for 4 + 3 they count out four, then three, then start again from one and count the whole pile. Counting on is the first real leap — you keep the bigger number in your head and count up from it. For 4 + 3 you say ‘four… five, six, seven.’

The trick worth teaching alongside it is to start from the bigger number. Adding 2 + 9 by counting on from 2 is nine hops; from 9 it is only two. Children find this genuinely delightful once they notice 2 + 9 and 9 + 2 land in the same place. That idea — that order does not matter in addition — is a Grade 1 milestone in its own right.

2. Number bonds to 10

If a Grade 1 child knows the pairs that make ten — 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 — the rest of primary arithmetic gets easier for years. I would spend more time here than anywhere else on this list. Use a ten-frame (two rows of five squares) and ask ‘how many more to fill it?’ every day for a couple of weeks until the answers come without counting.

Why bonds beat memorisation

A child who has memorised that 7 + 3 = 10 knows one fact. A child who understands the bond knows that 3 + 7, 10 − 3, and 10 − 7 are the same picture. Bonds are the difference between one fact and four.

3. Making ten to cross the ten-line

This is the strategy that finally retires the fingers. To add 8 + 5, you borrow 2 from the 5 to complete the 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3: 8 + 5 becomes 10 + 3 = 13. It leans directly on the number bonds from strategy 2, which is why bonds come first.

It feels like a stretch at first. Model it out loud with counters and a ten-frame for a week before you expect a child to do it alone. When it clicks, sums like 7 + 6 and 9 + 4 stop being scary.

4. Doubles and near-doubles

Children memorise doubles — 3 + 3, 4 + 4, 5 + 5 — surprisingly happily, maybe because they sound like a chant. Once doubles are secure, near-doubles come free: 6 + 7 is just 6 + 6 and one more. Teaching 6 + 7 as ‘double 6, plus 1’ is far kinder than counting on seven times.

5. Adding zero and adding one

Do not skip the easy rules. ‘Adding zero changes nothing’ and ‘adding one gives the next number’ are two facts that remove a whole column of questions from a worksheet with almost no effort. They also quietly build the idea that numbers have a fixed order — the seed of the number line.

How the strategies fit together

StrategyBest forExample
Counting onSmall second number6 + 2
Number bonds to 10Anything that makes ten4 + 6
Making tenCrossing ten (sum 11–18)8 + 5
Doubles / near-doublesEqual or almost-equal numbers7 + 8
Add 0 / add 1The easy wins9 + 1

A realistic weekly routine

Ten minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday. A pattern that has worked for parents I know: two days on bonds to ten, two days on making ten, one day on doubles, and the weekend for mixed practice on paper so the child has to choose a strategy rather than being told which one. That choosing step is where real fluency shows up.

One honest caveat: do not chase speed too early. A child who reasons out 8 + 5 in four seconds is in a far stronger position than one who has rote-memorised it but cannot explain why. Speed comes on its own once the thinking is sound.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly these strategies — counting on, bonds to ten, making ten, and doubles. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 1 Addition Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions covering counting on, number bonds, making ten and doubles. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Start from the bigger number, 6, and count on three: 7, 8, 9.
4 and 6 fill a ten-frame exactly. The bonds to ten are 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 and 5+5.
Make ten: take 2 from the 5 to turn 8 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.
This is a double. Double 7 is 14.

questions.q: 6 + 7 is the same as which of these?
questions.explanation: 6 + 7 is a near-double: double 6 is 12, and one more makes 13.

questions.q: Which sum gives the same answer as 3 + 8?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter in addition, so 3 + 8 and 8 + 3 both equal 11.

questions.q: A child has 9 marbles and wins 4 more. How many now?
questions.explanation: Make ten: take 1 from the 4 to turn 9 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.

faq.q: At what age should a child master Grade 1 addition?
faq.a: Most children are 6 to 7 during Grade 1. By the end of the year the aim is fluent addition within 20 using strategies rather than finger-counting. Some get there sooner, some a term later — both are normal.

faq.q: Should I let my child count on fingers?
faq.a: Yes, at the start — fingers make the maths concrete. The goal is to give them better tools (bonds to ten, making ten) so they choose to leave fingers behind, not to ban them.

faq.q: What is the single most useful thing to practise?
faq.a: Number bonds to ten. A child who instantly knows the pairs that make ten finds making-ten, subtraction and place value far easier for years afterwards.

faq.q: How much daily practice is enough?
faq.a: About ten focused minutes a day, mixing a strategy drill with a few written questions, beats a long weekly session. Consistency matters more than length at this age.
